To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
(i) Ca2+ is involved in the control of iodide efflux from thyroid cells and (ii) Ca2+ can oppose the action of cAMP on iodide influx.

(1) TSH and cAMP increase intracellular iodide levels in FRTL-5 thyroid cells, (2) TSH increases intracellular Ca2+, (3) cAMP and Ca2+ increase iodide uptake into FRTL-5, and (4) Ca2+ increases iodide efflux from FRTL- 5.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the mechanisms involved in thyroid hormone synthesis and release.
the study of the role of Ca2+ as a second messenger in the control of thyroid function.
the role of Ca2+ ions in the control of thyroid cell function, in particular the role of Ca in regulating the transport of iodide into and out of the thyroid cell.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
Ca(2+) is involved in the regulation of the thyroid iodide transport process, but its role is complex and not yet fully understood.
Ca2+ plays an important role in the regulation of thyroid iodide metabolism.

(1) the thyroid cells in question have two functionally distinct processes that regulate the level of iodide within the cell; (2) the process that is stimulated by cAMP and TSH is the one that brings iodide into the cell; (3) the process that releases iodide from the cell is stimulated by Ca++ (and possibly alpha-adrenergics); and (4) Ca++ and cAMP are not antagonists in the control of iodide transport.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

Ca2+ plays a role in the regulation of the iodide efflux process in thyroid cells and that the effects of Ca2+ on this efflux process may be independent of the effects of cAMP on the iodide influx process.
the effects of Ca2+ on iodine transport are complex and depend on the cell model used.
Ca2+ is an important second messenger in the regulation of thyroid cell function and may act in concert with cAMP in the control of the intracellular iodide concentration.
The main takeaway from our work is that
we were able to demonstrate the presence of a novel, non-cyclic-AMP-dependent mechanism of TSH action on the thyroid gland.
Ca2+ is involved in both the stimulation of iodide uptake by TSH, as well as the efflux of iodine from the cells.
